modules.title: Meet BFS
goals: Explain what BFS is for, and when it is the right tool.
Trace BFS by hand: say which vertex comes next, what is in the queue, which vertices are visited and the order they are visited in.

segments.title: Your turn: predict every step
segments.body:
Open the BFS visualiser on the campus graph: **[predict every step](/graphs/4)**.

Before each step, pick the vertex BFS takes next.

- Look at the queue panel, not the graph: BFS always takes the vertex at the **front** of the queue.
- Alphabetical order only decides the order neighbours **join** the queue, not which vertex leaves next.
- A vertex that hasn't joined the queue yet can't be next.

segments.title: Worked example: filling in a trace table
segments.body:
We trace BFS on the campus graph from **A**, one row for each vertex that leaves the queue. A vertex is **found** when it joins the queue, and BFS never adds a vertex it has already found. It is **visited** when it leaves the queue, which is when it joins the order.

| Step | Current vertex | Queue after the step | Visited | Order so far |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| start | – | A | – | – |
| 1 | A | C, E | A | A |
| 2 | C | E, B, F | A, C | A, C |
| 3 | E | B, F, D | A, C, E | A, C, E |

**Step 1.** A leaves the queue, so it is visited and joins the order. Its neighbours in alphabetical order are C and E. Neither has been found yet, so both join the back of the queue.

**Step 2.** C is at the front, so C leaves. Its neighbours are A, B and F. A has been found already, so only B and F join.

**Step 3.** E leaves. Its neighbours are A, D and F. A is visited, and F is already waiting in the queue, so only D joins.

The remaining steps work the same way. The full order is **A, C, E, B, F, D, G**.

segments.title: Worked example: a vertex that is already waiting
segments.body:
Here is a whole trace on a new graph, with one tricky step. The graph is undirected, with vertices M, N, P, Q, R and S, and edges M–S, N–Q, N–R, P–R, Q–S and R–S. We start at **Q**. A vertex is **found** when it joins the queue, and **visited** when it leaves.

| Step | Current vertex | Queue after the step | Visited | Order so far |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| start | – | Q | – | – |
| 1 | Q | N, S | Q | Q |
| 2 | N | S, R | Q, N | Q, N |
| 3 | S | R, M | Q, N, S | Q, N, S |
| 4 | R | M, P | Q, N, S, R | Q, N, S, R |
| 5 | M | P | Q, N, S, R, M | Q, N, S, R, M |
| 6 | P | (empty) | Q, N, S, R, M, P | Q, N, S, R, M, P |

**The hard step is step 3.** S leaves the queue. Its neighbours, in alphabetical order, are M, Q and R. Q is visited already. R hasn't been visited, but it is **already waiting** in the queue: it was found at step 2, so it doesn't join again. Only M is new, so only M joins the back.

**For each row, ask three things.** Which vertex is at the front? It leaves and is visited. Which of its neighbours haven't been found yet? Those join the back, in alphabetical order.

**Explain it to yourself before you go on:** at step 4, R leaves, and its neighbours are N, P and S. Why does only P join the queue?

segments.title: Worked example: is BFS the right tool?
segments.body:
Is BFS the right tool? Ask two questions.

**Question 1. Is there a graph?** Are there things joined to other things? If not, there is nothing for BFS to search.

**Question 2. What does the problem ask for?** BFS reaches vertices in rings: first everything one edge from the start, then everything two edges away, and so on. So it is the right tool for **the fewest edges** to somewhere, or **everything within a number of edges** of a start. It counts edges, so it is not the right tool when each edge has its own length or cost.

| Problem | 1. A graph? | 2. What is asked? | BFS? |
|---|---|---|---|
| The fewest clicks from one web page to another | Yes: pages joined by links | The fewest edges | Good fit |
| The quickest drive, when each road takes a different number of minutes | Yes: places joined by roads | The least total time, not the fewest roads | Not a fit |
| The highest mark in a test | No: the marks aren't joined | – | Not a fit |

**Explain it to yourself before you go on:** a drive along more roads can still be quicker. Why does that rule BFS out for the quickest drive?

segments.title: Try another: is BFS the right tool?

config.prompt: The walkways on campus can be used in both directions. What kind of graph is the campus map?

options.label: It is not a graph, because walkways have different lengths

feedback.b: A directed edge only goes one way, like a one-way street. These walkways go both ways.
feedback.c: Edges can have lengths (weights) and still be a graph. Here we only care whether two buildings are connected.

hints.body: Think back to module 1: what is the difference between a directed and an undirected edge?
A directed edge has an arrow and can only be followed one way.
Can you walk from A to C and also from C to A? Then the edge has no single direction.
Answer: an undirected graph, because every walkway can be used in both directions.

activities.title: Quick recall: a graph in Python

config.prompt: Using the `Graph` class from module 2, an empty undirected graph runs `add_vertex("A")`, `add_vertex("C")` and then `add_edge("A", "C")`. What is `adjacency` now?

feedback.b: That is a directed edge from A to C. In an undirected graph C must also list A.
feedback.c: Each vertex maps to a list of neighbours, and both A and C are in the dictionary.

hints.body: Remember how module 2 stored an undirected edge.
Each vertex has a list of its neighbours.
If A is a neighbour of C, then C is also a neighbour of A.
Answer: {"A": ["C"], "C": ["A"]} — the edge is stored once in each vertex's list.

activities.title: When is BFS the right tool?

config.prompt: For each situation, choose whether BFS is a good fit and why.

left.label: Find the route between two stations on the Gautrain map with the fewest stops.
List everyone who is a friend, or a friend of a friend, of Thandi on a social network.
Add up the prices of all items in a shopping list.

right.label: Good fit: BFS reaches vertices in order of the fewest edges from the start.
Good fit: BFS explores one ring of neighbours at a time, so it finds everyone within two steps first.
Not a fit: there are no connections to follow, so this is not a graph problem.

feedback.s3: A list of prices has no vertices and edges to traverse. A simple loop is enough.
feedback.s1: Fewest stops means fewest edges. That is exactly the order in which BFS reaches vertices.
feedback.s2: Friends are one edge away, friends of friends two edges. BFS finds them ring by ring.

hints.body: First ask: are there things connected to other things? If not, it is not a graph problem.
BFS explores everything one edge away, then everything two edges away, and so on.
'Fewest stops' and 'friend of a friend' are both about counting edges from a start.
Answer: s1 → r1 (fewest stops), s2 → r2 (ring by ring), s3 → r3 (not a graph).

activities.title: Already confident? The queue after C

config.prompt: Already confident? On the campus graph from A, after C is processed, what is in the queue (front first)?

feedback.b: E was already waiting. New vertices join at the back, so E stays in front.
feedback.c: B and F join together at the back, after E.

hints.body: What was in the queue before C was processed?
C leaves from the front, and C's new neighbours join at the back.
Before: C, E. C leaves. B and F join behind E.
Answer: E, B, F.

activities.title: Trace BFS from B: one row each time a vertex leaves the queue

hints.body: Start with only B in the queue. Nothing is visited yet. Row 1 is what happens when B leaves.
For each row: take the vertex at the front of the queue. It is now visited and joins the order. Then add its neighbours that haven't been found yet, in alphabetical order, at the back of the queue.
Row 1: B leaves, and its neighbours A and D join. Row 2: A leaves. Its neighbours are B and C, and only C is new.
Answer: the order is B, A, D, C, E. The queue after each row is [A, D], [D, C], [C], [E], []. At row 3, C is not added again because it is already waiting in the queue.

config.prompt: On the campus graph, what is the fewest number of walkways from the Admin block (A) to the Green (G)? Use the BFS order you found: A, C, E, B, F, D, G.

feedback.b: 6 is G's position in the order, not its distance. Follow who discovered whom back to A.
feedback.c: G is not joined to C or E. It needs one more walkway, from B.

hints.body: Ask: which vertex added G to the queue?
B added G. Which vertex added B?
C added B, and A added C. Count those walkways.
Answer: 3 walkways, A → C → B → G.

activities.title: Try another: trace BFS from F, one row each time a vertex leaves the queue

hints.body: Start with only F in the queue. Nothing is visited yet. Row 1 is what happens when F leaves.
For each row: the vertex at the front leaves and is visited. Its neighbours that haven't been found yet join the back, in alphabetical order.
Row 1: F leaves, and D and H join. Row 2: D leaves. Its neighbours are E and F, and only E is new. Row 3: H leaves. E is already waiting in the queue, so nothing joins.
Answer: the order is F, D, H, E, G. The queue after each row is [D, H], [H, E], [E], [G], [].

activities.title: Try another: is BFS the right tool?

config.prompt: For each problem, choose whether BFS is a good fit and why.

left.label: Find the fewest moves a chess knight needs to get from one square of the board to another.
In a video game, find every room of a castle that is no more than two doors from the entrance.
Plan the trip between two towns that uses the least petrol, when every road uses a different amount.
Count how many learners in a class wrote the test.

right.label: Not a fit: BFS counts edges, but here each edge has its own length or cost.
Good fit: the first time BFS reaches a vertex, it has used as few edges as possible.
Good fit: BFS takes neighbours in alphabetical order, so it sorts the answer.
Not a fit: nothing is joined to anything, so there is no graph to search.
Good fit: BFS has found everything one edge away before it finds anything two edges away.

feedback.s1: Not quite. The squares are vertices and each knight move is an edge, so the fewest moves is the fewest edges from the start. Look for the reason about the fewest edges.
feedback.s2: Not quite. The rooms are vertices and the doors are edges, and no more than two doors means everything within two edges. Look for the reason about one ring of neighbours at a time.
feedback.s3: Not quite. There is a graph, but each road uses its own amount of petrol, and BFS only counts edges: a trip along more roads can still use less petrol. Look for the reason about each edge having its own length.
feedback.s4: Not quite. Counting learners needs no connections between them, so there is no graph and nothing for BFS to search. Look for the reason that says there is no graph.

hints.body: First ask: are there things joined to other things? If not, there is no graph.
Then ask what the problem wants: the fewest edges, everything within some number of edges, or the least total length?
BFS counts edges and works ring by ring. It ignores lengths, and alphabetical order only decides which neighbour joins the queue first.
Answer: knight → the fewest edges; castle rooms → one ring at a time; least petrol → each edge has its own length; counting learners → no graph to search.
